summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a child protection agency to protect a child from violence by a private actor, so the agency's failure to remove the child was not a constitutional violation.
key_cases.relevance: DeShaney controls the threshold question in every child-fatality case in which the child remained in or was returned to parental custody.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.case_name: White Ex Rel. White v. Chambliss
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held South Carolina DSS officials were entitled to qualified immunity on claims arising from the removal of children and the foster placement in which one child died, because no clearly established federal right — including any right created by the South Carolina Child Protection Act — was violated.
key_cases.relevance: White governs the federal claim arising from a child's death under agency supervision in this jurisdiction.
key_cases.quote: The facts presented by White reveal that the DSS defendants violated no "clearly established" law in removing White's children from her custody.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal, holding South Carolina's child abuse reporting statute creates a duty owed to the public and no private cause of action for failing to report, and that no common law duty to warn future victims existed.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the narrow special-duty exception under which a DSS worker, unlike a private reporter, may owe a duty to an individual child.
key_cases.quote: The fact that such language is missing from § 20-7-510 indicates the legislative intent was for the reporting statute not to create civil liability.

key_cases.case_name: Jensen ex rel. Estate of Clark v. Anderson County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals, adopting the six-element special duty exception to the public duty rule and holding that the Child Protection Act imposes on the local child protection agency and its social workers a special duty to investigate and intervene whose breach may give rise to a private cause of action, with immunity turning on remand on whether the duty breached was ministerial or discretionary.
key_cases.relevance: Jensen is the controlling South Carolina authority recognising the special duty exception for a child who dies after an agency failure, and it is the counterweight to the defense-side authority that otherwise fills this node.
key_cases.quote: the Act imposes a special duty on the local child protection agency and its social workers to investigate and intervene in cases where child abuse has been reported
